newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan position on yen still a mystery ahead of G7.
newsitem.headline: Japan position on yen still a mystery ahead of G7.

text.p: Japanese financial officials have kept silent as to whether they want Saturday's meeting of Group of Seven nations to act to check the sharp fall of the yen.

The officials have made no secret of their desire for a G7 commitment to currency stability, but whether Tokyo seeks formal cooperation by the world richest economies to stop a further, relentless fall by the Japanese currency remains a mystery.
Finance ministers and central bankers from the G7 -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- are to meet in Berlin on Saturday.
The dollar hit a high of around 124 yen in Tokyo on Thursday, a stunning 55 percent recovery from its record low of 79.75 yen in April 1995.
Monetary sources have declined to comment on whether Japan will ask its G7 allies to formally endorse a cap on the dollar/yen rate.

They will only say that Japan will stress the importance of foreign exchange market stability, echoing Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka's repeated comments that an excessive weakening or strengthening of the yen are undesirable.

Previously, Tokyo had expressed some concern over the dollar's quick rise, saying it would spike up Japan's contentious trade surplus and result in currency volatility or trigger another steep rise in the yen in the future.
A strong dollar or a weak yen makes American goods more expensive on global markets, while boosting competitiveness of Japanese products.
But monetary officials have toned down such comments as the yen's depreciation improves earnings of the export sector, providing a quick fillip to the nation's fragile recovery.

Germany does not seem too concerned about the current dollar level either, as it also gives its exports a boost at a time when Bonn's ability to use fiscal stimuli for growth is limited by its struggle to meet budget criteria of Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

Yet concern over a weaker yen still lingers among Japanese bureaucrats, as it has prompted and may again trigger a slide in Tokyo share prices. A stock market tumble could choke Japan's still fragile economy by discouraging spending and by slowing the pace of bad loan write-offs by Japanese banks.
U.S. monetary authorities, meanwhile, have not shown any signs of changing their stance that a strong dollar is in the best interests of the United States.

Earlier this week, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin brushed aside U.S. exporters' complaints about the strength of the dollar, saying that the United States should not use the dollar as an instrument of trade policy.
Japanese officials are more forthcoming with clues on what may turn into a tussle with the United States on the need for measures to keep Japan's economic recovery going.
Tokyo is likely to stand by its plan to sharply tighten its budget policy but to fend off possible pressure for it to do more to spur growth, monetary officials said.
The United States has been urging Tokyo to continue fiscal and monetary stimuli to sustain its domestic-demand-led economic recovery.
A senior official at Japan's Ministry of Finance (MOF) told Reuters: "Putting off Japan's budget consolidation would hardly be beneficial to sustainable growth of the global economy."
An international monetary source, who declined to be identified, said on Wednesday that Japan and Europe may share a similar policy stance when it came to budget reform.
He said Europe's strong drive to cut back its budget deficit to meet the tough criteria for EMU amid only moderate growth would eventually pay off.
"Our understanding is that policy efforts to reduce the budget deficit steadily over the medium-term will eventually ensure a firm basis for growth."
Japan's state and local government debt is the worst among the G7 countries, accounting for about six percent of its gross domestic product.
